routes.description: Establish that possible conscious experiences and the causal relations among them are factual features of reality capable of supporting objective distinctions between better and worse ways for conscious beings to live.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if facts about consciousness identify genuine differences in well-being, permit discoverable navigation among possible states, and remain normatively significant despite contingent preferences and the first-person character of experience.

motionBridge.description: Show that facts about conscious well-being can ground objective evaluative guidance rather than merely implement independently chosen ends.

centralBridges.description: Establish a factual landscape of possible conscious states containing materially better and worse conditions and causal routes between them.
Explain why inherited or modifiable preferences do not exhaust the standards by which possible changes in experience are evaluated.
Connect discoverable facts about navigating conscious experience to objectively right and wrong practical directions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for the reality of values instantiated in consciousness despite their essentially first-person mode of appearance.
Allow for attainable goods that agents may fail to recognize because of empirical cognitive, emotional, or cultural limitations.

routes.description: Establish that ethical language expresses attitudes or directives while science supplies objective information only about how conscious systems can realize ends selected through subjective preferences.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if preferences, including higher-order preferences, can explain the selection of ends and if empirical facts can explain effective pursuit of those ends without entailing objective moral truth, obligation, or prescription.

motionBridge.description: Show that emotive expression plus instrumental facts can account for ethical discourse and practical coordination without objective morality.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish expressing an attitude through moral language from reporting a truth-apt fact about possessing that attitude.
Separate subjective selection of experiential ends from objective scientific knowledge about the means of attaining them.
Explain preference change, cooperation, flourishing, and informed action without introducing objective moral properties or prescriptions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for voluntary alteration of preferences through higher-order desires rather than an independent moral standard.
Locate value in the commitments of conscious systems while preserving objective facts about effective action.

sections.title: The semantic status of ethical language
sections.rationale: The dispute requires an account of whether moral utterances state objective propositions, report subjective states, or instead express attitudes and directives.

sections.title: Experiential landscapes and the ends-means distinction
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether factual knowledge of possible conscious states and causal routes establishes evaluative destinations or only serves antecedently selected ends.

sections.title: Preference revision and higher-order desire
sections.rationale: The treatment of contingent and scientifically alterable preferences determines whether preference change requires a further evaluative standard or remains preference-relative.

sections.title: Subjective experience and the reality of value
sections.rationale: The debate turns partly on whether value's first-person manifestation undermines objectivity or identifies a real feature of conscious systems that facts can track.

sections.title: Practical flourishing and objective moral direction
sections.rationale: This issue asks whether a complete practical account of cooperation, discovery, flourishing, misery avoidance, and experiential navigation entails objective moral direction.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Possible conscious experiences extend beyond what agents currently prefer or can access, and factual knowledge can identify routes among experientially different states.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: Present preference weights arise from unchosen genetic, familial, and cultural causes and could themselves be altered by a mature science of mind, leaving the desirability of such changes open for evaluation.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Refusing the language of should and ought does not establish that nothing evaluative hangs on attainable changes, because failure to recognize how good life could become may reflect empirically identifiable cognitive or cultural closure.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: Some realities exist essentially as appearances in consciousness and cannot be conceptually reduced to external physical descriptions, even if they can be correlated with physical states; their first-person character therefore does not make them unreal.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-001.proposition: Even in simple social conditions, actions open or close possibilities for collaboration and produce discoverably different experiential outcomes, permitting objectively better or worse navigation when better means movement away from the worst possible misery.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Ethical pronouncements express attitudes or commands rather than truth-apt propositions about objective moral facts.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: An emotivist moral utterance expresses a feeling rather than factually reporting that the speaker possesses that feeling.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Science can identify how to reach a desired experiential peak while the desire to reach that peak remains a subjective preference.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: Voluntary preference enhancement can be explained by higher-order preferences without introducing moral goodness, obligation, or prescription.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: Conscious systems have subjective values, while objective facts concern how best to achieve what those systems subjectively value.

chunk-001:c010.proposition: Preference, cooperation, discovery, and scientifically informed flourishing can form a complete practical account without objective moral truth.
